adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:197 — Switching live `span-buf:s:*` keys from sets to sorted sets without a migration makes new ZADD/ZSCAN/ZCARD calls fail with WRONGTYPE during rolling deploys and for all pre-deploy keys until expiry.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a clear change from Redis SET operations (sadd, scard, sscan, sunionstore) to SORTED SET operations (zadd, zcard, zscan, zunionstore) in buffer.py. The Lua script add-buffer.lua also changes from scard/sunionstore to zcard/zunionstore. During a rolling deployment, old code instances will still use SET commands while new instances use SORTED SET commands on the same keys. Redis will return WRONGTYPE errors when SET commands are executed against SORTED SET keys and vice versa. Additionally, any existing keys created before deployment will be SETs, and the new code's SORTED SET operations will fail on them until they expire.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:840 — The optimized audit-log paginator passes a datetime to math.ceil/floor, so any authorized `optimized_pagination=true` request with results raises TypeError instead of returning a page.

src/sentry/api/paginator.py:880 — A caller-supplied negative cursor offset reaches Django queryset slicing even though Django rejects negative indexes, turning the advertised advanced path into a 500 response.
matched_golden_ids: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the same problem as the golden comment. Both point out that in OptimizedCursorPaginator's get_result() method, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset is negative, the negative offset is passed directly to Django queryset slicing. The candidate adds the consequence (Django rejects negative indexes causing a 500 error), but it's fundamentally the same underlying issue about negative cursor.offset being used directly in queryset slicing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:47 — ZUNIONSTORE's default SUM aggregation inflates timestamps for duplicate payloads present in both merged sets, allowing replayed old spans to survive eviction ahead of genuinely newer spans.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows ZUNIONSTORE being used at lines 47 and 52 in add-buffer.lua without specifying an AGGREGATE option. By default, Redis ZUNIONSTORE uses SUM aggregation, which means if the same payload (member) exists in both sets being merged, their scores (timestamps) will be added together. Since the scores represent end_timestamp_precise values (as shown in buffer.py line 196-198 where zadd uses end_timestamp_precise as the score), summing timestamps for duplicate payloads would produce incorrect, inflated timestamp values. This could cause the zpopmin eviction at line 58 to remove wrong spans - spans with legitimately recent timestamps could be evicted while duplicates with artificially inflated scores survive. The correct behavior would require AGGREGATE MIN or MAX to preserve meaningful timestamp ordering.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:30 — Reducing redirect traversal from 10,000 to 1,000 silently splits deeper span trees without detecting that the redirect chain was truncated.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the loop limit being reduced from 10,000 to 1,000 at line 30. The original code had a comment stating 'theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' By reducing this to 1,000, deeper span trees (between 1,000 and 10,000 depth) that previously would have been correctly joined will now be silently truncated. The code doesn't add any detection or logging when the redirect chain is truncated at the new lower limit, meaning data could be silently split without any indication.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py:79 — The opt-in paginator treats the datetime ordering field as numeric, so any nonempty optimized audit-log request fails while building cursors instead of returning the documented response.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows OptimizedCursorPaginator extends BasePaginator and uses get_item_key() which calls getattr(item, self.key) and applies math.floor/ceil to the value. When used with order_by='-datetime' on audit logs, self.key would be 'datetime' which is a datetime object, not a numeric value. Calling math.floor() or math.ceil() on a datetime would raise a TypeError. The DateTimePaginator (the original paginator) likely has special handling for datetime fields, but OptimizedCursorPaginator treats all values as numeric. This is a real bug that would cause the optimized pagination path to fail.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:877 — A caller-supplied optimized cursor with a negative offset reaches unsupported negative Django queryset slicing and produces a server error instead of a valid page or rejected cursor.

adjudication.rationale: The diff at lines 875-880 in src/sentry/api/paginator.py shows that when `enable_advanced_features` is True and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` (a negative value) and then does `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django querysets do not support negative slicing - this will raise a ValueError or AssertionError. The code comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' but this is incorrect. A malicious or buggy client could supply a negative offset cursor value and cause a server error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:197 — ZADD raises WRONGTYPE for still-live span buffers created as Redis sets by the previous version, breaking ingestion during a rolling deployment or for up to the one-hour buffer TTL afterward

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a migration from Redis SET commands (sadd, scard, sscan) to SORTED SET commands (zadd, zcard, zscan) in buffer.py. In line 197, the code now uses p.zadd() instead of p.sadd(). The Lua script in add-buffer.lua also changes from sunionstore/scard to zunionstore/zcard. During a rolling deployment, old keys created as SETs will still exist in Redis (with TTL up to the set_timeout). When the new code tries to execute ZADD on an existing SET key, Redis will return a WRONGTYPE error because you cannot use sorted set commands on a set data type. This is a real backward compatibility issue during deployment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:840 — The optimized audit-log path passes datetime values to math.floor/math.ceil, so every nonempty optimized response raises TypeError instead of returning results
matched_golden_ids: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue identifies exactly the same problem as the golden comment: the OptimizedCursorPaginator's get_item_key method uses math.floor/math.ceil on datetime values, which causes a TypeError. Both comments point to the same bug - datetime objects being passed to floor/ceil functions that don't support them.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:882 — A caller-supplied negative cursor offset reaches Django queryset slicing even though Django rejects negative slice bounds, producing a server error rather than pagination

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces OptimizedCursorPaginator with code at lines 879-883 that explicitly allows negative offsets when enable_advanced_features is True: 'start_offset = cursor.offset' (allowing negative values) followed by 'results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])'. Django querysets do not support negative slice indices and will raise an AssertionError or ValueError. The comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' which is false - Django explicitly rejects negative indices in queryset slicing. This is a real bug that would cause server errors when a user with advanced features enabled provides a negative cursor offset.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:30 — Capping redirect traversal at 1001 lookups can attach a span to an intermediate buffer and split a deep trace because redirect chains can exceed the 1000 retained payloads across incremental batches

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows two related changes: (1) the redirect traversal loop limit was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations in add-buffer.lua line 30, and (2) a new span count limit of 1000 was added with zpopmin to cap retained payloads. The finding correctly identifies that these limits interact problematically - if a trace has deep redirect chains that exceed 1000 lookups, spans may be attached to intermediate buffers rather than the correct root. Combined with the 1000 span limit that removes older spans via zpopmin, this could cause trace fragmentation. The concern is valid because the redirect depth limit and span count limit are now aligned at 1000, but redirect chains can legitimately grow across incremental batches as spans arrive out of order.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:62 — The hard-coded 1000-span cap ignores SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans, so configured limits are no longer honored and larger configured segments are silently truncated

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a hard-coded limit of 1000 spans in the Lua script (line 62: `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)`). Looking at buffer.py, there is a `max_segment_spans` attribute used in the SpansBuffer class (visible in the removed code around line 446-452 that checked `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`). The Lua script now enforces a hard-coded 1000 limit that cannot be configured, which means any configured `max_segment_spans` value larger than 1000 will be silently ignored and segments will be truncated to 1000 spans.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:197 — Reusing the existing span-buf:s key namespace for ZADD makes this code incompatible with SET-valued keys left by old or concurrently deployed workers, so version the key schema or provide a rolling migration

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a change from SET operations (sadd, scard, sunionstore, sscan) to SORTED SET operations (zadd, zcard, zunionstore, zscan) on the same key pattern 'span-buf:s:{project_and_trace}:{parent_span_id}'. In buffer.py line 197, the code now uses p.zadd() instead of p.sadd(). If there are existing Redis keys created by the old code using SET data type, the new code attempting SORTED SET operations on those keys will fail with a WRONGTYPE error. The finding correctly identifies this as a compatibility issue requiring key versioning or migration strategy.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:62 — The eviction cap is hardcoded to 1000 while SpansBuffer still exposes an unused max_segment_spans setting, so pass one authoritative limit into the script or remove the dead configuration

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a configuration inconsistency. The diff shows the Lua script hardcodes 1000 as the span limit (line 62: `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000)`), while the Python code in buffer.py still has `max_segment_spans` as a configurable setting (visible in the removed code at lines 446-452 that checked `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`). The removal of the Python-side check while adding a hardcoded Lua-side limit creates a disconnect where the Python configuration becomes dead code. This is a legitimate architectural concern about configuration consistency, not a bug since the system will still function.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:845 — OptimizedCursorPaginator copies nearly all of BasePaginator.get_result, forcing pagination fixes to be maintained twice instead of isolating the offset policy behind a small override

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that OptimizedCursorPaginator (lines 818-912) duplicates nearly all the logic from BasePaginator.get_result method. Looking at the diff, the new class copies the entire get_result implementation including cursor handling, queryset building, hit counting, offset calculation, and result processing - with only a small difference in how negative offsets are handled (lines 875-883). This is a legitimate architectural/maintainability concern: any future bug fixes or improvements to the base pagination logic would need to be applied in two places. The finding is specific, grounded in the actual diff code, and represents a real maintenance burden introduced by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:63 — ZPOPMIN materializes every evicted payload in the Lua VM, so a large batched insert can allocate and process the entire overflow while blocking Redis; delete the rank range without returning members instead.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that ZPOPMIN at line 63 returns the removed members, which means Redis must serialize and return potentially many payloads when span_count exceeds 1000 significantly. The diff shows `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)` which would return all evicted members. Using ZREMRANGEBYRANK would be more efficient as it only returns the count of removed elements, not the elements themselves. This is a valid performance concern for the new code, though not a correctness bug - the code will work, just with unnecessary memory allocation in Redis's Lua VM.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py:71 — The advanced audit-log path treats the persistent superuser flag or project-wide access as administrator authorization, allowing use without an active superuser session or an administrative org role.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows on line 71: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. This check uses `is_superuser` which is a persistent flag on the user model, not an active superuser session check. In Sentry's security model, superuser access typically requires an active session (checked via `is_active_superuser()`). Additionally, `has_global_access` on a member indicates organization-wide project access, not administrative privileges. The OptimizedCursorPaginator with `enable_advanced_features=True` allows negative offset pagination which could potentially expose data beyond normal pagination bounds. This is a security concern where the authorization check is too permissive.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py:126 — All added score fixtures are identical and contain at most five spans, so no test verifies the 1,000-span boundary or that eviction retains the newest timestamps.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a 1000-span limit with eviction logic in add-buffer.lua (zpopmin when span_count > 1000), but the test fixtures all use identical timestamps (1700000000.0) and contain only 4-5 spans each. No test verifies the boundary condition at 1000 spans or that eviction correctly retains spans with the highest timestamps. This is a valid concern about missing test coverage for newly added nontrivial logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua:47 — No test merges sorted sets containing the same payload, leaving ZUNIONSTORE's score aggregation and its effect on eviction order unverified.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a change from Redis SETs (SADD/SUNIONSTORE) to sorted sets (ZADD/ZUNIONSTORE) in both the Lua script and Python code. ZUNIONSTORE with the default AGGREGATE SUM behavior will add scores when the same member exists in multiple sets. The finding correctly identifies that there are no tests verifying behavior when the same payload appears in multiple sets being merged - all test cases use distinct span payloads. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for the new sorted set implementation, though it's not a bug since duplicate payloads in different sets would be an edge case. The finding is specific and grounded in the actual diff changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:840 — No nonempty audit-log integration test exercises this paginator, which applies math.floor to a datetime and will fail while building the first response cursor.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key() at line 840 applies math.floor/math.ceil to `value = getattr(item, self.key)`. When used with audit logs ordered by '-datetime', self.key would be 'datetime', and the value would be a datetime object. Calling math.floor() on a datetime will raise TypeError. The finding correctly identifies this as a bug - the paginator is designed for numeric values but is being used with datetime fields in the audit log endpoint. The lack of integration tests means this would fail at runtime.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/paginator.py:882 — No negative-offset boundary test covers the advanced branch, which passes a negative slice to a Django QuerySet even though Django rejects negative indexing.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces OptimizedCursorPaginator with code at lines 879-884 that explicitly allows negative offsets when enable_advanced_features is True: 'start_offset = cursor.offset' (allowing negative values) followed by 'results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])'. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and will raise an AssertionError. The finding correctly identifies this as a bug - the code path allows negative slicing which Django rejects. The comment claims 'Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' which is false.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py:71 — The new permission-sensitive paginator selection has no endpoint tests proving opt-in is denied to ordinary members and enabled only for the intended administrator roles.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces new permission-sensitive logic at line 71-73 that checks `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` to enable advanced pagination features. This is security-sensitive code that determines which users can access the OptimizedCursorPaginator with `enable_advanced_features=True`. The finding correctly identifies that there are no endpoint tests in the diff verifying this permission check works correctly - that ordinary members are denied and only administrators get access. The test files modified in the diff are for spans/buffer functionality, not for the audit logs endpoint. This is a legitimate concern about missing test coverage for newly added permission-sensitive logic.
